vignette: John is a 49-year-old North American male and an architect who witnessed a violent incident at his workplace several months ago. The traumatic event occurred during a routine meeting in which he was present when a colleague unexpectedly attacked another employee with a knife. The sudden violence left John feeling shaken, as he struggled to process the intense emotions and physical reactions triggered by the event. Since then, certain triggers have significantly impacted John's daily life. Whenever he smells scents reminiscent of that day or feels nauseous, the memories of witnessing the violent scene resurface. These sensory triggers are particularly potent because they remind him vividly of the traumatic event, reigniting his fear and unease. For example, when he catches a whiff of cologne similar to what the attacker was wearing, John immediately recalls the terrifying moment. John's threat perceptions have intensified as a result of these triggers. He feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall where he can see everything in the room, constantly scanning for exits whenever he enters any new space. This heightened vigilance stems from the persistent fear that another violent incident could happen at any moment. John's startle response has also become more pronounced; even minor sounds now cause him to jump or feel on edge. The trauma has left John with fragmented and disordered memories of the event, making it difficult for him to piece together a coherent narrative. He knows what happened but struggles to find words to describe his experience accurately. When he does remember the frightening incident, he feels as though it is happening all over again, which further exacerbates his anxiety. John's negative appraisals have significantly influenced his reactions and behavior since the traumatic event. He believes there is something inherently wrong with him that made the event happen and feels isolated from others, unable to share or discuss what he experienced. These internalized beliefs contribute to his heightened sense of threat. John often thinks that bad things are inevitable and that he cannot prevent them from happening again. John's negative appraisals also reinforce his triggers; for instance, his belief that there is something inherently wrong with him makes the sensory reminders more impactful and distressing. This self-reinforcing cycle has made it increasingly difficult for John to function in both his personal and professional life. His obsessive scanning of exits and back-to-wall positioning are now habitual responses whenever he steps into any new environment, including work meetings or social gatherings. John's inability to articulate what happened during the traumatic event compounds his distress; the fragmented memories leave him feeling vulnerable and constantly on guard. As a result, John has become more isolated from colleagues and friends, avoiding social interactions where he might encounter potential triggers. These behaviors have taken a toll on John's relationships and work performance. He finds himself increasingly reluctant to participate in team meetings or visit client sites due to the heightened risk of encountering sensory reminders or feeling unsafe. This avoidance has strained his professional relationships and led to several missed deadlines, causing significant stress at work. Ultimately, what brought John to seek help was a growing sense that he could no longer manage the overwhelming feelings of fear and isolation on his own. He is most afraid of being alone with his thoughts and memories but also harbors hope for regaining control over his life and finding a way to process his experiences without constant fear. John's current state is marked by a deep-seated belief that he cannot prevent bad things from happening, which further fuels his anxiety and sense of isolation. He hopes therapy can help him find a path toward healing and reclaiming his sense of safety and connection with others.
